resources.string:
A light meter assumes everything is middle grey — Zone V. Point it at snow and it underexposes until the snow is grey; point it at a black coat and it overexposes until the coat is grey.

The Zone System turns that from a flaw into a tool. Spot-meter one thing that matters, decide which zone it should land on, and shift the exposure to put it there. Each zone is one stop. Skin in sun usually sits well on Zone VI (one stop over the reading), textured snow on VII, a dark shadow you still want detail in on III.

Then meter the shadows and the highlights to see what the rest of the scene will do. More than about seven stops between them and something will fall off the film: on negative film, protect the shadows and let the highlights go; on slide film, the other way round.

Exposure is meant to be a trade: half the light for twice the time. On film that trade stops holding for long exposures. Below about a second, the emulsion responds less to dim light than the arithmetic says, so a metered 10 seconds needs 15, 30 or more.

Every stock fails differently. Modern T-grain films like Delta and T-Max hold up well; older cubic-grain films like Tri-X and HP5 fall away faster; colour films can also shift colour, because the three layers fail at different rates.

The manufacturers publish curves or a formula, usually corrected time = metered time to a power between about 1.3 and 1.5. When in doubt, bracket long, not short: negative film forgives a stop of overexposure far more readily than it forgives thin shadows, and the shadows are what reciprocity eats first.

Pushing is underexposing on purpose — shooting ISO 400 film at 1600 — and making up for it with longer development. Pulling is the reverse: overexpose, develop less.

It is not free. A push does not add shadow detail the film never recorded; it raises contrast and grain, and shadows thin out. That suits dim, flat light. A pull lowers contrast and softens grain, which suits harsh light.

The whole roll is developed together, so it is shot at one speed from first frame to last. Mark the canister clearly, and tell the lab how many stops — "push +2" — when you drop it off. Labs often charge for it, and some will not push slide or colour film beyond a stop or two.

Developing yourself, start from the push times on the developer's data sheet. Black-and-white films like Tri-X and HP5 push two stops gracefully; most colour negative film takes one.

In the hour after sunrise and before sunset, light reaches the ground through more atmosphere. Blue scatters out, so what is left is warmer, and the low angle throws long shadows that show texture and shape.

The light also changes fast. A reading that was right five minutes ago may be a stop off now, so meter again before each frame rather than trusting the last one. On colour negative film the warmth is part of the look; on slide film it shows exactly as it was, so a warming filter is rarely needed.

Side light flatters faces and landscapes; backlight gives rim light and flare. For backlit portraits, meter the face, not the sky, and accept that the background will burn out.

The "hour" is shorter near the equator and longer near the poles, and in winter far north it can last most of the day.

A meter is only ever right about middle grey. Most scenes average out close enough, and that is why metering usually works — but some scenes do not.

Backlit subjects, snow, beaches and white walls fool it into underexposing. Night scenes with a few bright lights, black cars and dark interiors fool it into overexposing. Give a stop or two more than it says for the first group, less for the second.

A spot reading of the thing that matters, placed where you want it, beats any average. Failing that, meter something mid-toned in the same light — grass, grey stone, the back of your hand plus one stop — and use that.

Negative film has latitude: a stop or two over is usually fine, under rarely is. Slide film has almost none, and wants exposure for the highlights. When the light is tricky and the frame matters, bracket.

Every mount has a flange distance: how far the lens mount sits from the film. A lens can only focus to infinity on a body whose flange distance is the same or shorter than the one it was designed for.

That is why M42 screw-mount lenses adapt so well — 45.46 mm — to bodies with shorter registers, with a thin adapter making up the difference. Going the other way needs glass in the adapter to restore infinity, and that glass costs sharpness.

M42 on a Nikon F body is the awkward case: Nikon's 46.5 mm is longer than M42's, so plain adapters lose infinity focus and only work close up.

Adapted lenses often lose the automatic aperture. Many M42 lenses have an A/M switch: set it to M so the aperture closes as you turn the ring, then meter stopped down. The viewfinder gets darker, but the reading is right.

Stand development uses very dilute developer — Rodinal at 1+100 is the classic — and a long time, usually an hour, with agitation only at the start, and sometimes once halfway.

With so little agitation, developer exhausts quickly next to dense highlights and keeps working in the thin shadows. That compensates: highlights hold back, shadows come up, and edges sharpen where the two meet. It is forgiving of mixed exposures and of films shot at different speeds on one roll.

The risks are uneven development and bromide drag — streaks below sprocket holes and dense areas, where exhausted developer sinks. Use enough developer per roll (many people want at least 5 ml of Rodinal concentrate per 135 roll), tap the tank to dislodge bubbles, and keep the temperature steady.

Semi-stand adds a gentle agitation at the halfway point to cut the drag.

In bright sun, set the aperture to f/16 and the shutter speed to one over the film's ISO — 1/125 for ISO 100, 1/400 or 1/500 for ISO 400. No meter needed.

The rule scales with the light. Slight overcast, soft shadows: f/11. Overcast, barely any shadows: f/8. Heavy overcast: f/5.6. Open shade or sunset: f/4. Snow or sand in full sun: f/22, because the ground reflects so much.

Any equivalent exposure works. f/8 at 1/500 lets in the same light as f/16 at 1/125, so pick the pair that suits the depth of field or the motion you want.

It is a starting point, not a law. It assumes front light on an average subject. Backlight, deep shadow or a pale subject still need judgement — but on a sunny day with a dead meter battery, it will get you good negatives.
